doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Memorable players: Cleo Laine, Charlie Haden, Ed Blackwell
summary: Blackwell was the biggest influence; the Mighty Lights recording and a Vanguard week.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You’ve been able to — in addition to having your own band — played with quite a list of people, and I wonder if there’s been some folks that have stood out in your mind as being really memorable experiences.

Oh a lot. And for different reasons too. Working with Cleo Laine — some kind of special feeling I had about playing with her, and it meant a lot to me. Playing with Charlie Haden and Ed Blackwell was probably the most exciting rhythm section I’ve ever worked with in my life, and I played the Village Vanguard with them. I mean I will never forget Blackwell, ever. I think Ed Blackwell, of the instrumentalists, Ed Blackwell probably had a more profound influence on me, absolutely, not because we talked about anything, but completely musically. It was just completely about music communication of what he did and what I played with him, and what happened when we played, that I’ll never forget. I don’t think I’ve ever felt a cymbal like that in my life again, since he passed away.
Was that a fairly spontaneous gig too?

Well I recorded with them on Enja Records in the early 80s. And it was a recording that I was asked to pick whatever rhythm players I wanted to record with and they were them. And it included pianist Fred Hersch and a number of festival appearances and concert appearances happened after that recording. It was called “Mighty Lights” and at the time it got a lot of attention, and the most exciting for me, opportunity, was to play a week at the Vanguard with this group. So I always remember that.
